Attention Trading Partners: MIHMS Upgrade October Payment Cycle Changes and System Access Limitations

Sep 21, 2026

As previously communicated, the Office of MaineCare Services (OMS) is preparing to launch an upgraded version of MIHMS, MaineCare’s claims processing system. The upgrade is currently scheduled to go live on October 10, 2026. To support a smooth transition, OMS must implement temporary system access limitations and adjustments to payment cycles in October.  

From Friday, October 2 at 8:00 PM until Monday, October 12 at 8:00 AM, MIHMS will be in a “data freeze” while OMS completes final system readiness and transition activities. 

Please note that we have updated the FAQ previously shared, as of September 21, 2026. 

Changes to October payment cycles:   

Review this information and plan billing accordingly to prepare for the transition.    

Payment Cycle Date 

Type of Cycle 

Claim Submission Deadline for Inclusion in Payment Cycle* 

Wednesday, 9/30/26  

Last regular payment cycle before the data freeze  

Friday, 9/25/26, 5:00 AM 

Thursday, 10/1/26 

Extra payment cycle before the data freeze 

Wednesday, 9/30/26, 5:00 AM 

There will be no payment on Wednesday, October 7. 

Thursday, 10/15/26 

First payment cycle after data freeze, in upgraded system 

Secure File Transfer Protocol (SFTP) submission: Continuous through data freeze up to Tuesday, 10/13/26, 2:00 PM 

  

Portal submission: 

Before data freeze: Friday, 10/2/26, 7:59 PM 

After data freeze: Tuesday, 10/13/26, 2:00 PM 

Wednesday, 10/21/26 

Regular payment cycle, in upgraded system 

Friday, 10/16/26, 5:00 AM 

  *As always, timely submission does not guarantee that the claim will process in time for the next payment cycle. OMS may take up to 30 days to process and pay a claim, depending on any edits or issues that may cause the claim to pend for manual review, as well as other processing requirements that may require the full 30-day timeframe. 

Preparing for the changes to October payment cycles: 

The HealthPAS Online Portal has returned to its previous regular operating hours. Providers again have 24/7 access to the portal, for additional flexibility and time to submit claims outside of standard business hours.   

We strongly encourage providers to submit claims approaching timely filing limits in the next few weeks to avoid potential submission delays. The planned data freeze does not modify existing Medicaid timely filing requirements. Providers remain responsible for ensuring claims are submitted within the established timely filing guidelines. 

Other system access limitations: 

Providers can find other expected impacts of the data freeze in this FAQ. We have updated the FAQ as of September 21, 2026. Topics include: 

  • HealthPAS Online Portal, including impacts on submitting claims, submitting prior authorizations, and checking member eligibility 
  • Provider Enrollment Application (PEA) 
  • Value-Based Purchasing Management System (VMS) Portal 
  • Paper & fax document submissions 
  • Provider Services & Member Services call centers 
  • Value Added Network (VAN) Trading Partners 
  • Prior authorizations for prescriptions and behavioral health services 
  • Electronic Visit Verification (EVV) 
  • Secure File Transfer Protocol (SFTP) 

You can also check the OMS Provider Resources webpage, in the first box of information called “Health PAS Online Portal,” for the most recent information about the upgrade.  

For questions or clarifications, please contact Provider Services at 1-866-690-5585. Please note, Provider Services does not have additional information beyond what is shared in this message and in the FAQ linked above.

Attention Trading Partners: Training for New MaineCare Partner Portal

Sep 21, 2026

We have previously shared that a refreshed and upgraded MIHMS, with a new “MaineCare Partner Portal,” is coming in October 2026. This will replace the current HealthPAS Online Portal. We are now inviting trading partners to register for training that began September 8, 2026 to help you prepare for the transition to the new portal. Trading partners include providers, billing agents, health plans, clearinghouses, and business associates. Trading partners have an important role to play in supporting a smooth transition and uninterrupted access to the portal after go-live. 

Gainwell Technologies will be leading live virtual instructor-led training sessions. These courses will provide the knowledge and skills needed to navigate the new portal, complete daily business functions, and use new portal features. Training demonstrations, materials, and supporting resources will help participants prepare for a successful transition. 

Steps you need to take to attend training 

  • Review the available training topics listed below and identify the sessions that align with your role and responsibilities. 
  • Use the LMS registration (instructions below) to create an account, access the training catalog, and enroll in applicable sessions. 
  • Contact Gainwell (instructions below) if you need assistance. 
  • Recorded sessions and other training materials will be available in the LMS after training sessions for ongoing reference. 

MaineCare Partner Portal Training Sessions 

Course Name 

Description 

ME - TPT - Migrated Trading Partner Log In and Account Maintenance Training (ILC) 

Learn how to complete first-time login activities, configure multi-factor authentication (MFA), manage user accounts and permissions, perform account maintenance activities, and understand electronic data interchange (EDI) certification requirements and status monitoring. This course is only for Admin (R7) users. 

ME - TPT - Trading Partner Registration and Account Maintenance Training (ILC) 

Learn how to register a new Trading Partner account, complete account activation, manage users and permissions, associate providers and billing agents, navigate the portal, and maintain account information.  

ME - TPT - Authorization, Referrals and Certifications Training (ILC) 

Learn how to submit and manage authorizations, process referrals, monitor certification requests and statuses, and access related portal functionality. 

ME - TPT - Dental Claim Entry & Claim Management Training (ILC) 

Learn how to submit dental claims, monitor claim processing and status, and navigate claim-related portal functions. 

ME - TPT - Institutional Claim Entry & Claim Management Training (ILC) 

Learn how to submit institutional claims, monitor claim processing and status, and navigate claim-related portal functions. 

ME - TPT - Professional Claim Entry & Claim Management Training (ILC) 

Learn how to submit professional claims, monitor claim status, review payment information, access remittance advice, and complete related claim activities. 

ME - TPT - MaineCare Partner Public Portal Training (ILC) 

Learn about publicly available portal functionality, portal resources and reference materials, secure messaging, Trading Partner tools, and available resources.

  3. If you need a new account, enter the enrollment key: De8pO9CBYXYB-aOCY8qp on the Sign Up window. 
  4. Complete the required registration information to create your account. Note: You can enter your workplace address. 
  5. The Learner Dashboard appears. From this window, you can access previous trainings, search for and enroll in the appropriate training sessions, and review your transcript. 
  6. To locate the appropriate courses, search using “TPT” or the course name from the table above in the search bar at the top of the window or by opening the Course Catalog tile.

    • Access the Teams Meeting hyperlink from the course confirmation email. 
    • Click the Microsoft Teams meeting hyperlink within the Outlook/Teams calendar event. 
    • Access My Courses in the LMS and click the appropriate Microsoft Teams meeting hyperlink.

Maine's Minimum Wage to Increase to $15.70 Per Hour in 2027

September 18, 2026

For Immediate Release: September 18, 2026

Media Contact: Autumn Mahoney, Communications Specialist media.dol@maine.gov

AUGUSTA - The Maine Department of Labor announced today that, effective January 1, 2027, the state minimum wage will increase from $15.10 to $15.70 per hour, based on data recently made available by the U.S. Department of Labor's Bureau of Labor Statistics. MDOL is required under Maine law (Maine statute Title 26, chapter 7, section 664) to make annual adjustments to the minimum wage based on the cost-of-living index (CPI-W) for the Northeast Region, after Maine voters amended the law by referendum in 2016. Between August 2025 and August 2026, there was a 4.1 percent increase in the CPI-W.

According to the U.S. Department of Labor's Bureau of Labor Statistics Current Population Survey for 2025, there were 28,000 hourly workers who were paid less than $15.00 per hour. These workers represent about four percent of all wage and salary workers (both paid at hourly rates and not paid at hourly rates) and about eight percent of wage and salary workers who are paid at hourly rates.

Agricultural workers in Maine are also entitled to the state minimum wage, after the Legislature enacted and Governor Mills signed "An Act to Establish a State Minimum Hourly Wage for Agricultural Workers" in 2025.

The "tip wage," or service employee minimum wage, will increase from $7.55 to $7.85 per hour. This means that service employees must receive a direct cash wage of at least $7.85 per hour from the employer. The employer must be able to show that the employee receives at least the minimum wage of $15.70 per hour when the direct wage and tips are combined at the end of the week. The amount of tips necessary to qualify as a service employee will increase from $191 to $199 per month.

The minimum salary threshold for exempting a worker from overtime pay must exceed 3,000 times the State's minimum wage or the annualized rate established by the U.S. Department of Labor, whichever is higher. Starting January 1, 2027, the new minimum salary threshold for salaried workers exempt from overtime will be $905.79 per week, or $47,101.08 per year. This is only one of the factors used in determining whether a worker is exempt from overtime pay under federal or state law. An individual can earn more than the minimum salary threshold and still be eligible for overtime. The duties of each worker must be considered as part of this analysis.

Employers can download the required minimum wage poster at no cost on the Department's website.

The minimum wage and overtime law can be found here.

More information about minimum wage and other labor standards is available on the Department's website

Hello, this is Governor Janet Mills, and thank you for listening.

You know, when I took office nearly eight years ago, I promised that Maine won't wait to take action to protect our state, our people, and our economy from the dangers of extreme weather events caused by pollution and changes to our environment. And I promised that we would fight to preserve this special place that we call home; preserve it for the benefit of our children and grandchildren.

The stakes could not be higher. Look no further than the devastating storms of just a few years ago. Storms that impacted our communities, our people, and our economy—that destroyed a lot of infrastructure across the state.

I've made climate action a cornerstone of my Administration. First, we created the Maine Climate Council, and we issued a groundbreaking climate action plan. And we dedicated millions of federal and state dollars to make that plan a reality.

In 2025, we made the single largest investment in storm recovery by any administration in Maine history, and we created the State Resilience Office to build better, stronger public infrastructure to withstand future storms.

That office manages a partnership of more than 300 communities and has awarded more than $29 million in state and federal funds for projects to prepare local communities for flooding, for storm surge, for rising sea levels, and other climate and weather events that put people's lives and livelihoods at risk.

Recently, I was proud to announce the latest round of funding through that partnership: more than $4.7 million in grants to 72 cities and Tribal Governments, including the towns of Bingham and Madawaska:

  • The Town of Bingham will install high-efficiency heat pumps and a rooftop solar system in order to lower their energy costs at the municipally owned Veterans Building;
  • The Town of Madawaska will use their grant to launch the RIDER Program, a shared e-bike fleet in a rural community that doesn't have public transportation;
  • And the Town of Freedom will use its grant to do an energy audit of its buildings and to plan for a bridge replacement across Hustus Brook.

Through these projects and so many more, we are continuing to address the very real threat of severe weather events for the health of our people, the health of our environment, and the health of our economy.

You know that clean air and clean water know no political party. Our planet is neither Democratic nor Republican. It's the home of all of us, and it is the responsibility of all of us and all governments to preserve it for future generations.

I am proud that over the past nearly eight years, we've made cost-effective heat pumps, weatherization programs, and other things available for Maine people and businesses. We've attracted investments in emerging industries and renewables, and we've created good-paying, green collar jobs. We've reduced our reliance on expensive fossil fuels, and we've mobilized scientists, industry leaders, local and state officials, and young people from all over to act as one to address the effects of climate change.

We won't wait for the next storm or the next disaster. We do care. And as the author Wendell Berry wrote, "We care for this home that is ours. A home that we care for as we care for no other place in the world."

This is Governor Janet Mills, and thank you for listening.

Contact: Mark McInerney, (207) 620-0197

The 3.2 unemployment rate in August changed little from July. Nonfarm wage and salary jobs have remained within a narrow range for 28 consecutive months.

The 3.2 percent unemployment rate changed little from recent months. Unemployment rates have remained within a narrow range between 3.1 and 3.3 percent for 24 consecutive months. Unemployment has been below 4 percent for 56 months, the longest duration on record. Maine's unemployment rate has been below the U.S. average for more than 18 years, and remains below the long-term average of 5.4 percent for the state since 1976. Unemployment averaged 4.1 percent for New England and 4.1 percent for the U.S. in the month.

The labor force participation rate averaged 58.8 percent over the last three months, lower than during the three months through May. A decreasing employment-to-population ratio in the three months through August is the primary reason for lower rates of labor force participation.

Seasonally Adjusted Statewide Nonfarm Jobs Estimates

Preliminary seasonally adjusted estimates indicate that in August, nonfarm wage and salary jobs were little changed from July. Employment levels were stable in every sector.

Job estimates have stayed within a narrow range near 660,000 for 28 consecutive months (estimates ranging less than 0.5 percent higher or lower each month). Over the last year, job increases in the health care and social assistance, and retail trade sectors were offset by modest decreases across several sectors.

Not Seasonally Adjusted County and Metro Area Labor Force Estimates

On a not seasonally adjusted basis, the statewide unemployment rate was 3.1 percent. Rates were at least 0.3 percentage points higher than that in seven counties, at least 0.3 points lower than that in four, and close to the average in five. Rates were lowest in the coastal counties and highest along the northern rim of the state.

Among the three metro areas, unemployment was below the statewide average in Portland-S. Portland, and close to the average in Bangor and Lewiston-Auburn.

Not Seasonally Adjusted Statewide and Metro Area Hours and Earnings Estimates

The private sector workweek averaged 33.5 hours and earnings averaged $33.77 per hour in August. Average hours changed little, and hourly earnings increased 4.2 percent from one year ago. The workweek was longest in the construction and manufacturing sectors and shortest in the leisure and hospitality sector. Earnings were highest in professional and business services and lowest in leisure and hospitality. Hourly earnings were above the statewide average in Portland-S. Portland and below it in the Bangor and Lewiston-Auburn metros.

Sep 18, 2026

items.title: Secretary of State marks Constitution Day with unveiling of official printing of Maine Constitution — Maine Secretary of State — Bureau of Corporations, Elections & Commissions News
items.content_text:
First printing since 1876 includes redacted indigenous treaty obligations
AUGUSTA, MAINE
– Secretary of State Shenna Bellows marked Constitution Day by formally unveiling the official printing of the Maine Constitution, the first formal printing since 1876. The unveiling took place at the Maine State Cultural Center in Augusta and included displays of the original 1820 copy of the Maine State Constitution and the 1876 version along with the new printing.
For more than a century, Maine omitted three original sections – Sections 1, 2 and 5, of Article X of the Constitution – from official printed copies. The sections, which remained in full force despite the redaction, include treaty obligations to the Wabanaki tribal nations. In 2023, Mainers voted overwhelmingly to cancel the 1876 amendment compelling the redaction and restore the language to printed copies of the constitution.
“Restoring this language to the Maine Constitution is a visible and lasting reminder of the important role the Wabanaki people played in the formation of Maine,” said Secretary Bellows. “The Wabanaki have existed in Maine for 13,000 years, and voters made it clear that their immeasurable contributions to our collective past, present and future should be known, acknowledged and celebrated, not hidden from history.”
The large format version was printed using a 19th century letterpress onto vellum by Wolfe Editions of Portland and will be permanently housed at the Maine State Archives along with the previous versions.
###

Welcome to the online digital collection of the Maine State Archives, a bureau within the Department of the Secretary of State. We maintain approximately 8 miles of official state records (both paper and digital) that are deemed permanently valuable. These records include bills introduced in the Legislature, reports from the Governor's Executive Council, election returns, deeds and maps from the Maine Land Office, vital statistics prior to 1892, federal census records up to 1880, county court records dating back to 1636, and military records through World War I, among others.
As of March 1, 2026, our online collection includes over one million individual records. The Maine State Archives will continue to expand this database as we digitize more of our collection. , the logging industry creates rural jobs and provides revenue for local communities, contributing $534 million to the state’s economy annually; and
WHEREAS
, loggers provide renewable material for products used by people in Maine every day; and
WHEREAS
, loggers are the root of Maine’s $8.3 billion forest economy; and
WHEREAS
, loggers are the means by which healthy and responsible forest management plans are accomplished; and
WHEREAS
, logging helps keep Maine’s forests healthy, which support vital animal habitats, protect watersheds, sequester carbon, provide recreational opportunities, and limit wildfires; and
WHEREAS
, logging provides for healthy forests through regeneration to ensure the sustainability of the industry for future generations of Maine people;
NOW THEREFORE
, be it resolved that I, Janet T. Mills, Governor of the State of Maine, do hereby proclaim October 12, 2026 as
Maine Logger’s Day

the Great Seal of the State to be
hereunto affixed GIVEN under my
hand at Augusta this tenth day
of September Two Thousand Twenty-Six

, named after a popular preacher of that era, George C. Needham, the Needham candy consists of a mashed potato center surrounded by coconut and chocolate; and

, it is thought that Needhams gained popularity with home cooks during the Great Depression, when Maine people would use their extra potato harvest to make the treat; and
WHEREAS
, Needhams have become synonymous with Maine, and they help celebrate locally harvested Maine potatoes; and

, be it resolved that I, Janet T. Mills, Governor of the State of Maine, do hereby proclaim September 26, 2026 as
Maine Needham Day

Sep 16, 2026

The Maine Department of Health and Human Services’ Center for Disease Control and Prevention (Maine CDC) is reporting a case of measles in Maine; the first case in the state since five cases were confirmed in February of this year. The Maine CDC confirmed the latest case on September 15, 2026. According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (U.S. CDC), as of September 11, there were 3,294 confirmed measles cases reported nationwide in 2026.

The individual is an unvaccinated adult from Somerset County. The Maine CDC is working with the facility where potential exposure occurred and is working with them to inform potentially exposed individuals.

Individuals who were at the following location* during the timeframe listed below were potentially exposed to measles and should take precautions and should watch for symptoms for 21 days after September 12:

Location

Date

Time

MaineGeneral Express Care, Waterville 211 Main Street, Waterville, ME

September 12, 2026

8am-11am

*Subject to change as the investigation continues

Measles is a highly contagious viral disease. If one person has measles, 90% of the people close to that person who are not immune will become infected. Symptoms of measles include:

  • Fever
  • Cough
  • Runny nose
  • Red, watery eyes
  • Rash that spreads from the head down.

Individuals who develop symptoms should contact their health care provider for instructions before going to the provider’s office or hospital. This will help prevent the spread of further infection. If symptoms are consistent with measles, a health care professional may test to determine a measles infection.

Measles can cause severe sickness including pneumonia, encephalitis (brain swelling), and death. An infected person spreads measles through coughs or sneezes. Once infected, a person is contagious from four days before their rash starts through four days afterwards. The virus remains alive for up to two hours on surfaces and in the air. The period from exposure to onset of symptoms is typically 10 to 14 days, but can be longer.

The measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine is the best prevention for measles. Individuals who:   

  • have been potentially exposed should review their vaccine history and watch for symptoms.
  • are not immunized or do not know their measles immunization status should get vaccinated.
  • develop symptoms should contact their health provider for instructions before going to the provider’s office or hospital. This will help prevent the spread of further infection.

Recommendations: 

  • Children – Identify and vaccinate children who are not up to date with their MMR vaccines. All children should receive two doses of MMR vaccine. A health care professional should administer the first dose to children at 12 to 15 months old and the second at 4 to 6 years old.
    • Children 6 to 11 months old who will be traveling internationally or domestically to a region with a known active measles outbreak should receive one dose of MMR vaccine, per the Maine CDC’s expanded recommendations for those traveling to a destination with a known outbreak. This dose is not considered part of the routine two-dose series starting at age 12 months.  
  • Adults – All adults should have proof of immunity to measles. Acceptable proof includes one of the following:
    • written documentation of vaccination
    • laboratory evidence of immunity
    • birth before 1957
    • or laboratory confirmation of disease
    • individuals who received a measles vaccine between 1963 to 1967 are encouraged to speak with their doctor to determine if additional vaccination is needed. Those known to have received an inactivated dose measles vaccine should receive a single dose of MMR. Five percent of people who received measles vaccine between 1963 and 1967 received an inactivated vaccine.

For adults with no evidence of immunity to measles, the U.S. CDC recommends one dose of MMR vaccine as soon as possible. Adults who are traveling domestically or internationally to a region known to have an active measles outbreak should receive two doses of the vaccine. Pregnant women should not receive any live virus vaccine during pregnancy, including MMR.

Vaccination Information:

  • Two doses of MMR vaccine are about 97% effective at preventing measles; one dose is about 93% effective.
  • The U.S. CDC considers people who received two doses of MMR vaccine as a child protected for life. 
  • Some people exposed to the virus may still get measles even if they got the MMR vaccine. In this case, they are more likely to have a milder illness and are also less likely to spread the disease to other people.

For More Information:

  • The Maine CDC’s measles webpage: http://www.maine.gov/dhhs/measles
  • The U.S. CDC’s measles webpage: http://www.cdc.gov/measles/index.html
  • The Maine Immunization Program webpage: https://www.maine.gov/dhhs/mecdc/infectious-disease/immunization/

items.title: US Supreme Court Upholds Right to Vote by Mail — Maine Secretary of State — Bureau of Corporations, Elections & Commissions News
items.content_text:
AUGUSTA, MAINE
– Absentee voting by mail will continue just as it has in prior elections, announced Secretary of State Shenna Bellows today.  The US Supreme Court rejected the US Postal Service and Trump Administration’s quest to change the rules for mailed ballots.  States including the State of Maine had filed a lawsuit to challenge the Trump Executive Order and US Postal Service rule that would have dramatically limited the ability of clerks to mail ballots to voters.  A lower court blocked the rule on constitutional grounds, and the US Supreme Court denied the Trump Administration’s attempt to overturn the lower court.
“This is good news for voters and for democracy.  Voters can rest assured that they have all of the same options for absentee voting including receiving and returning their ballot by mail that they have had in every other election,” said Secretary of State Shenna Bellows.  “We know that many Mainers – particularly seniors and people with disabilities – appreciate the convenience of voting from home, and we are thrilled that our joint legal efforts with states across the country to protect the right to vote by mail have succeeded.”
Voters can request absentee ballots utilizing the Secretary of State’s online
absentee ballot portal
, in writing, or by calling their
municipal clerk
directly. Absentee voting in Maine begins October 5, and voters should start receiving their ballots in the mail in the first week of October. Voters can track the status of their absentee ballot via Maine’s
online absentee ballot tracking portal
.

“This is good news for voters and for democracy.  Voters can rest assured that they have all of the same options for absentee voting including receiving and returning their ballot by mail that they have had in every other election,” said Secretary of State Shenna Bellows.  “We know that many Mainers – particularly seniors and people with disabilities – appreciate the convenience of voting from home, and we are thrilled that our joint legal efforts with states across the country to protect the right to vote by mail have succeeded.”

Voters can request absentee ballots utilizing the Secretary of State’s online absentee ballot portal, in writing, or by calling their municipal clerk directly. Absentee voting in Maine begins October 5, and voters should start receiving their ballots in the mail in the first week of October. Voters can track the status of their absentee ballot via Maine’s online absentee ballot tracking portal.

items.title: US Department of Labor investigation finds Chicago construction employer exposed workers to continued safety hazards, proposes $265K in penalties — U.S. Department of Labor — News Releases
items.content_text: CHICAGO – The U.S. Department of Labor has cited a Calumet City-based residential construction and carpentry employer after two separate investigations into its continued failure to provide fall protection for workers. The department’s Occupational Safety and Health Administration investigated two worksites operated by Martin Araujo – doing business as Araujo Construction Corp. – and found that carpenters and general construction laborers were installing roof rafters and roof sheeting without fall protection, exposing them to falls of up to 25 feet. OSHA cited Araujo Construction with two willful violations for not providing fall protection, while working from heights during residential construction at the two worksites. OSHA also cited the employer with nine repeat safety violations for failing to provide head and eye protection, lacking handrails on stairways, and failing to make sure ladders extended three feet above access areas. Additionally, OSHA issued a serious violation to Araujo Construction for not having safe access to a platform, and an other-than-serious violation for lacking training certifications. OSHA proposed $265,868 in combined penalties.Martin Araujo has 15 business days from receipt of its citations and penalties to comply, request an informal conference with OSHA’s area director, or contest the findings before the independent Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission. Please check the OSHA establishment search page periodically for any changes in the inspection or penalty status.  Under the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970, employers are responsible for providing safe and healthful workplaces for their employees. OSHA’s role is to ensure these conditions for America’s working men and women by setting and enforcing standards, and providing training, education and assistance. See OSHA’s website for more information.

items.title: US Department of Labor debars Louisiana employer from H-2A visa program for federal violations — U.S. Department of Labor — News Releases
items.content_text: NEW ORLEANS – The U.S. Department of Labor debarred a Calcasieu Parish farmer from participating in the H-2A visa program for one year, after an investigation discovered multiple violations under the H-2A program.The department’s Wage and Hour Division determined that Jevon Natali, operating as Jevon Natali Farms near Lake Charles, violated H-2A program requirements when it misrepresented the actual terms and conditions of employment on its submitted job order. The H-2A visa program allows agricultural employers who anticipate a shortage of domestic workers to bring nonimmigrant foreign workers to the U.S. to perform agricultural labor of a temporary or seasonal nature. The one-year debarment prohibits the employer from hiring workers through the program during that period because of the seriousness of the violations.“Employers who abuse the H-2A program should expect to be held accountable for their actions,” said Wage and Hour Division District Director Troy Mouton in New Orleans. “Debarment sends a clear message that the Department of Labor will protect the integrity of this program and safeguard opportunities for American workers.”Division investigators also found Fair Labor Standards Act violations when Jevon Natali Farms failed to pay the required overtime premium of time-and-one-half employees’ regular rates of payfor non-agricultural work performed over 40 hours in a workweek. Jevon Natali Farms also failed to provide paystubs with the required information.Employees and employers can contact the Wage and Hour Division with questions and requests for compliance assistance at its toll-free helpline, 866-4US-WAGE (487-9243). Employers are encouraged to use the agency’s industry-specific compliance assistance toolkits to learn about their responsibilities under the laws enforced by the division.
